messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The accident happened on a Tuesday evening in late October. Maya was driving home from work, her mind already on the dinner she planned to make, when a pickup truck ran a red light and T-boned her sedan at the intersection. She remembers the sound of metal crumpling, the smell of gasoline, and the terrifying sensation of the car spinning before it came to a stop against a light pole. She had been conscious the entire time. In the moments after the impact, she sat frozen, her hands still gripping the wheel, watching a man in a blue jacket approach her window. She had not called 911 herself. She had not gotten out to check on the other driver. She had simply sat there, waiting, her body locked in place. In the weeks that followed, that stillness became the center of her shame.

Maya, a 25-year-old database administrator, began to avoid anything that reminded her body of the crash. She stopped jogging in the evenings, even though she had always enjoyed it, because the feeling of her heart pounding and her breath quickening felt too much like the aftermath of the collision. She started taking the elevator at work instead of the stairs. More quietly, she began to pull away from her friends. When they called to make plans, she found reasons to say no—she was tired, she had a deadline, she wasn't feeling well. What she did not tell them was that she could not bear the thought of sitting in a restaurant or a coffee shop and hearing someone call out a name that sounded like the man in the blue jacket, whom she later learned was named Mark. Hearing the name "Mark" in any context—on a television show, in a conversation at the next table—sent a jolt through her chest, and she could feel the entire scene of the crash replay behind her eyes, sharp and unwelcome.

She had come to believe that the accident was her fault. She told herself that if she had been paying more attention, if she had braked sooner, if she had done something differently, she could have avoided the collision entirely. This belief hardened into a more general mistrust. She began to feel that people could not be relied upon, that they were careless and dangerous, that the world was full of drivers who would run red lights and walk away without a second thought. When her husband, David, tried to comfort her, she found herself pulling away from him too, certain that he did not really understand, that he would eventually disappoint her.

The guilt and mistrust drove her deeper into isolation. She stopped answering her phone. She stopped checking her messages. When the silence became unbearable, she found herself in the bathroom, pressing the tip of a pair of scissors into her forearm hard enough to leave a mark. The sharp pain cut through the noise in her head, and for a few seconds, she felt nothing at all. She knew it was wrong, but she also knew it worked. And the more she did it, the more she believed she deserved it. The self-harm became a secret ritual, a way of punishing herself for her inaction, for not doing more to stop what happened. She would never forgive herself, she knew that.

The avoidance, however, only made the triggers worse. The less she went out, the more she noticed her own pulse, her own breathing, the small flickers of uncertainty in her daily life. A change in her work schedule, a delayed email from her manager, a road closure that forced her to take a different route home—every small unpredictability felt like a threat. Her body tensed. Her mind raced. The world felt unsafe, and she was certain that another disaster was waiting for her around the next corner. She began to monitor her environment constantly, scanning for signs of danger, for anything that could catch her off guard.

At work, she had always been meticulous, but now her caution bordered on paralysis. She triple-checked every database query, afraid that a single mistake would unravel everything. Her manager noticed the drop in her efficiency and asked if she was okay. Maya said she was fine. She was not fine. She had begun to avoid certain corridors in the office building because a coworker named Marcus worked on the third floor, and she could not bear to hear his name announced over the intercom. She took the long way to her desk, adding ten minutes to her commute through the building, telling herself it was for exercise.

What finally brought her to seek help was a night in early December. She had been lying in bed, unable to sleep, when David turned over and asked her, quietly, if she was still angry with him. She realized then that she had not spoken to him in three days. She had been avoiding him too. She was afraid of what he might say, afraid that he would confirm what she already believed—that she was broken, that she was to blame, that she had failed to do the one thing that mattered most. She agreed to see a therapist because she was terrified of losing him, and because she was even more terrified of what she might do to herself if she kept going the way she was.
